chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about the regurgitation (qals), and it is the belching (jush'a) by which food rises from the man's stomach without it being a full vomit, while he is standing in the Prayer. He (peace be upon him) said: 'That does not break his ablution, nor does it cut off his Prayer, nor does it break his Fast.'

key_terms.الْجُشْأَة: Belching; the act of belching which raises food
key_terms.الْقَلْس: Regurgitation; bringing food up from the stomach

ai.seo_question: Does regurgitation break wudu, prayer, or fasting?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Kafi, Samaanah ibn Mihar clarifies that *qals* (regurgitation) is distinct from full vomiting (*istirqaa*), establishing that the mere return of food to the mouth does not nullify ablution, prayer, or fasting. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on the completeness of the act rather than the mere sensation or partial return of contents, distinguishing it from the more stringent conditions often applied to full vomiting.
